knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: The patient is a 62-year-old Portuguese Caucasian female under observation at the Neurology Department of the Coimbra Hospital University Centre. Initial clinical signs appeared at the age of 12 with a gradual drooping of the right eyelid. At the age of 45, the left eyelid also became affected. During this period, she was seen for a corneal ulcer and reported having 'difficulties keeping her eyes open.' The condition has continued to progress slowly.. Confirmed diagnosis: Chronic Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia. Differential diagnosis includes: Chronic Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 42-year-old Italian woman reported a two-year history of drooping eyelids, limited eye movement, difficulty swallowing, reduced exercise capacity, and muscle pain. Laboratory tests revealed a slight increase in creatine kinase levels (243 U/L). Her parents were not related by blood, and there was no family history of neurological conditions. She had a past medical history of anxiety disorder. Physical examination indicated mild weakness in the muscles near the trunk of both the lower and upper limbs, weakness in facial muscles, drooping of both eyelids, and restricted eye movement.. Confirmed diagnosis: Chronic Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia and mitochondrial myopathy. Differential diagnosis includes: Chronic Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia and mitochondrial myopathy.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 34-year-old woman reported incomplete closure of the left eyelid and restricted eye movement for 8 years, with no relevant family history. She also experienced mild limitations in physical activity but did not seek immediate medical attention. Her parents are healthy and not related by blood. In 2017, she visited an ophthalmology hospital where fundoscopy and optical coherence tomography showed no abnormalities. She was prescribed oral pyridostigmine (60 mg tid) and prednisone (30 mg qd), but her symptoms did not significantly improve. The prednisone dosage was gradually reduced to 15 mg qd. In 2018, she experienced fatigue and weakness 6 months postpartum. In September 2019, she stopped taking pyridostigmine and prednisone due to a lack of noticeable improvement in her symptoms. In late 2020, she developed left-sided facial hypoesthesia. In 2021, her eye movement restriction worsened, particularly during the 8th month of pregnancy, accompanied by emotional stress, leading to retesting and strabismus.. Confirmed diagnosis: Chronic Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia. Differential diagnosis includes: Chronic Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 70-year-old female visited the glaucoma clinic for a follow-up on her glaucoma status. She had a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia, both managed with oral medications. Her ophthalmic history included a diagnosis of normal tension glaucoma 10 years prior, for which she was using dorzolamide twice daily and tafluprost once daily in both eyes. Physical examination showed symmetrical ptosis and facial atrophy. She reported a family history of eye movement issues affecting her father, brother, daughter, and herself from a young age. The patient declined genetic testing, but a family pedigree was established. Her best corrected visual acuity was 20/100 in the right eye and 20/80 in the left eye. Pupillary reflexes and Ishihara color test results were normal. Slit-lamp examination revealed bilateral cataracts, more pronounced in the right eye. Fundus examination showed minor pigmentary changes in both maculae. The optic discs had normal margins with peripapillary atrophy, and the cup/disc ratio was 0.7 in the right eye and 0.8 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was 10 mmHg in both eyes. knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 50-year-old male presented with hoarseness of voice for 18 months, worsening in the last 2 weeks, along with loss of appetite and weight loss. Six months ago, he experienced a dry cough and evening fever, and was treated for pulmonary tuberculosis. He has a 10-year history of chewing tobacco, but does not smoke, drink alcohol, or have a history of overseas travel. Clinical examination showed multiple large, tender, fungating lesions with necrosis on the tongue and three small, erythematous, non-tender papules on the forehead, which have been increasing in size over the past month. Basic laboratory investigations, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, hepatitis B surface antigen, anti-hepatitis C virus, and HIV 1/2 serology, were within normal limits and nonreactive. A chest X-ray revealed unilateral healed foci of patchy lesions. Sputum microscopy was negative for acid-fast bacilli, and the Mantoux test was positive. From all these considerations, it appears that the possible differential diagnosis of chronic FPIES is very wide. It also includes psychosocial (Munchausen by proxy syndrome, food aversion), neurological, and infectious (e.g. HIV, Salmonella, Yersinia) conditions. Although the clinical definition is vague, chronic FPIES is a factual entity in children not recognized for the syndrome, when they freely consume the offending food(s). In this situation, infants may incur the odyssey of FPIES.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 70-year-old African American male arrived at the emergency room with sudden right facial weakness and difficulty speaking that had persisted for five hours. He reported having non-fluctuating, progressive drooping of the eyelids for about 10 years and increasing difficulty swallowing liquids and solids over the past several months. His family history included bilateral ptosis in his father and paternal grandfather. Examination revealed symmetrical and bilaterally reactive pupils, severe bilateral ptosis, ophthalmoplegia with complete vertical gaze palsy, and severely restricted horizontal eye movements. Right-sided facial weakness affected the orbicularis oculi and oris muscles. Convergence was impaired, and there was difficulty with palatal elevation and swallowing. No muscle weakness was noted in the upper or lower limbs, and deep tendon reflexes were normal except for absent ankle jerks. The patient reported no pain. A brain CT scan showed no hemorrhage. A brain MRI the next day identified an acute ischemic stroke in the right dorsal pons at the level of the seventh cranial nerve nucleus and tract.
